content.text:
Below is a distilled “check-list” of what consistently works when you want an LLM-based agent to use all of its tools—rather than defaulting to a single favorite—and the design patterns that make those behaviors stick over time.

──────────────────────────────────
1. Curate the tool set before you prompt  
   • Fewer, cleaner tools beat a kitchen-sink inventory. Run a quick ablation test: remove each tool and see if task quality drops; keep only those that matter. ([huyenchip.com](https://huyenchip.com/2025/01/07/agents.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))  
   • Give each remaining tool a non-overlapping capability description and unique name (avoid two tools that both look like “search”). Ambiguous affordances are the #1 reason agents misuse tools.

2. Write an explicit “reason-then-act” rubric into the SYSTEM message  
   • Borrow the ReAct template: “First, think step-by-step about what you need. Then decide whether to call a tool; if so, which one; if not, answer directly.” ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/392094861_DESIGNING_NEXT-GENERATION_GENERATIVE_AI_AGENTS_FRAMEWORKS_MODELS_AND_PERFORMANCE_BOTTLENECKS?utm_source=chatgpt.com))  
   • Require the agent to output its internal chain-of-thought or a short “Plan” field before every action. This single instruction increases multi-tool diversity because the model must verbalize why the next tool is best instead of reflexively choosing the last one it used.

3. Give demonstrations for each tool—including edge-cases  
   • Example calls are stronger than prose descriptions. Provide at least one positive and one negative example for every function schema so the model learns boundaries as well as affordances.  
   • Keep JSON/function examples separate from natural language examples; mixing the two in one block confuses token-level patterns.

4. Add a “tool-selection checkpoint” wrapper  
   Pattern:  
   ① Agent produces Thought → ② A tiny wrapper prompt asks: “Does the plan require a tool? If yes, which?” → ③ Only then does the function call execute.  
   A May-2025 paper calls this the “Control Plane as a Tool” pattern; it cuts accidental over-use of a single tool and scales when the tool list grows. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06817?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

5. Log, measure, prune, repeat  
   • Track distribution of tool invocations and success/failure codes. Visualizing the histogram often reveals one or two “forgotten” tools; either improve their docs or delete them. ([huyenchip.com](https://huyenchip.com/2025/01/07/agents.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))  
   • Periodically fine-tune or RL-train on trajectories that score higher for (a) correctness and (b) balanced tool utility. The 2025 ARTIST framework shows 20 %+ gains from RL that explicitly rewards effective tool choice. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01441?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

6. Reward outcome quality, not mere tool usage  
   Penalize unnecessary calls (“dry runs”) and hallucinated parameters. Balanced agents learn that the cost of a wrong or pointless call is higher than the reward for making any call at all.

7. Use memories or retrieval to remind the agent what it can do  
   • On every new user turn, prepend a short, auto-generated “Tool Reminder” containing only the names + one-line purposes of tools that haven’t been used recently.  
   • Memory-augmented setups (vector or key-value) let the agent recall past successful patterns and diversify future choices. ([siddharthbharath.com](https://www.siddharthbharath.com/ultimate-guide-ai-agents/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

8. Keep schemas tight and deterministic  
   • Strongly type required/optional parameters and offer enumerated choices when possible; the more deterministic the schema, the easier it is for the model to see that “different questions → different schema shapes → probably a different tool.”

9. Provide a graceful fallback  
   If every tool call fails or times out, instruct the agent to (a) acknowledge the failure, (b) give its best direct answer, and (c) suggest trying the request again. This prevents loops where the model keeps hammering the same broken endpoint.

10. Evaluate end-to-end, not just step-wise  
   • Multi-hop tasks (e.g., “Look up stock price, then summarize CEO’s recent quotes, then draft an email”) reveal whether the agent can chain heterogeneous tools.  
   • Mixed-tool benchmarks are now appearing; include at least one in your evaluation suite so you don’t optimize for single-tool skill alone.

──────────────────────────────────
Minimal skeleton prompt that bakes the above in:

SYSTEM  
“You are an AI agent with the tools listed below.  
Always:  
1. Think step-by-step and state your Plan.  
2. Decide whether you need a tool call; if so, specify exactly one function with correct arguments.  
3. After receiving tool output, reflect: do you need another tool or can you answer?  
4. Prefer accuracy and brevity; avoid unnecessary tool calls.  
Available tools: …”

With curated tools, explicit reasoning scaffolds, checkpoint wrappers, and continuous telemetry, agents reliably learn to pick the right tool at the right time—rather than spamming the same familiar one.
